area: Artifact asset store — can it host a rendered voice clip at all
finding: NO, and the reason is the type list, not the size. `Artifact` publish with `asset: true` was called with the real decoded clip as vanessa-clip.mp3 and was refused outright, verbatim: `unsupported asset type ".mp3": publish with `asset: true` takes png, jpg, jpeg, gif, webp, svg, mp4, webm, pdf, woff2, woff, ttf, otf, csv, md, markdown, json, txt, ts, css, js, mjs, cjs.` There is no audio type on that list — not mp3, not m4a, not wav, not ogg. The `artifact-capabilities` skill's own description of the store agrees: 'image, SVG, video, PDF, font, or CSV/Markdown/JSON/text data'. Audio is simply not a thing the asset store accepts. Remuxing the MP3 into an accepted container (mp4/webm) was considered and NOT done: there is no ffmpeg in this environment, a hand-written ISO-BMFF muxer could not be tested for browser playback from here, and webm would force a re-encode off MP3. Proposing it would be inventing an untested mechanism.
evidence: One `Artifact` call, action publish, url https://claude.ai/artifact/EJnetbUCFscnDsDWFdp9Ti, file_path .../vanessa-clip.mp3, asset:true, on 2026-09-23. Error quoted verbatim above. `which ffmpeg ffprobe` returns nothing; `ffmpeg: command not found`.
fix: Recorded in integrations/vanessa-voice-everywhere.md under 'The link path — measured 2026-09-23'. The link design does not use the asset store; the clip rides in the page and in the artifact database instead (F-R4-04, F-R4-05).

area: Artifact asset store — the shape of the URL it returns
finding: SETTLED, and it kills the asset-URL idea a second time, independently of the type list. An asset URL is NOT a standalone URL. A 22-byte probe.txt was uploaded to the same artifact with an accepted type and the store returned the path `/_blob/bcd8de01541587fa24cfad17eb90e3bd` with the instruction 'Reference it from the page by that url verbatim ... which resolves in every view of the artifact'. That is a relative path. It has no host, no scheme and no meaning outside a view of the artifact that owns it. There is nothing there that could be pasted into an iMessage, a Discord message or a WhatsApp message — a recipient's browser has nowhere to send it. So even if the store had accepted audio, the thing it hands back is not a link. Any link Vanessa texts must therefore be the ARTIFACT PAGE URL (https://claude.ai/artifact/<id>), with the clip carried inside the page.
evidence: `Artifact` publish with asset:true of probe.txt (22 bytes, text/plain, sha256 ae544eeb...ae1b2) on 2026-09-23 against artifact EJnetbUCFscnDsDWFdp9Ti; response quoted above. The `artifact-capabilities` skill states the same shape independently: 'a stored id serves at "/_blob/" + id in every view'.
fix: Recorded in integrations/vanessa-voice-everywhere.md. The per-channel table names the artifact page URL, never an asset URL.

area: WHO CAN OPEN THE LINK — the decisive question
finding: ESTABLISHED, not assumed: the link is private, and that is the right answer for this use. Four independent lines agree. (1) The platform said so on every publish of the test artifact: 'readable by only you' and 'This artifact is private: only its owner and the people the owner has given access can open the link.' (2) The `artifact-capabilities` skill states that a page declaring the `assets` capability 'is organization-internal (never public)'. (3) An unauthenticated fetch from this session's sandbox, carrying no artifact credential, was REFUSED for both the page URL and the /_blob/ asset path: HTTP 403, 5,472 and 5,631 bytes of a Cloudflare 'Just a moment...' interstitial, no artifact content. (4) The strongest one, because it is a genuinely unrelated third-party server with no relationship to Steven's account: `inkbox_media_stage` with `source_type: "url"` — a mode whose own schema requires the URL be 'publicly reachable without credentials' — was pointed at the artifact URL and came back `url_fetch_failed: URL media could not be fetched safely`. Inkbox's servers cannot see the page. CONSEQUENCE, stated plainly: a link texted to Steven plays for Steven and for nobody else. Since the only permitted recipient of a voice reply is Steven himself, privacy is the feature. THE PRICE, equally plainly: the link only opens in a browser already signed in to that account, so on the phone it is the Claude app or Safari with a live session; a signed-out tap gets a sign-in wall, not the clip. WHAT IS NOT PROVEN: that a signed-in browser plays it. No browser was available in this session, so page load and audio playback were never observed — only that the bytes are present, correct and private.
evidence: Publish responses for artifact EJnetbUCFscnDsDWFdp9Ti, versions 1-3, 2026-09-23. `curl -sS -m 25 -o body -w 'http=%{http_code} type=%{content_type} size=%{size_download}'` against https://claude.ai/artifact/EJnetbUCFscnDsDWFdp9Ti and .../_blob/bcd8de01541587fa24cfad17eb90e3bd: both http=403, type=text/html, bodies beginning '<!DOCTYPE html><html lang="en-US"><head><title>Just a moment...</title>'. `inkbox_media_stage` {source_type:'url', purpose:'imessage', url:'https://claude.ai/artifact/EJnetbUCFscnDsDWFdp9Ti'} -> url_fetch_failed (invocation 7097fd20-5891-4689-9603-a1b1f2a81a63). Nothing was sent by that call; media_stage validates and stages without sending.
fix: Written up as its own section in integrations/vanessa-voice-everywhere.md and stated on the relay page itself, which tells its reader in plain words that the link is not a public link.

area: The clip inside the page — the mechanism that replaces the asset store
finding: PROVEN by execution. The full clip travels in the artifact page itself. The real 108,284 bytes were embedded as standard base64 in a `<script type="text/plain">` block and published privately as https://claude.ai/artifact/EJnetbUCFscnDsDWFdp9Ti. The published file is 158,484 bytes — 0.94 % of the 16 MiB page cap, about 106x headroom, the same order of comfort the 10 MiB iMessage cap gives the attachment path. The embedded base64 was decoded back out of the built file and hashes to sha256 747f8f5b869b6d24df6ad750eef2c38926a35f9265d0ef3089a8f8bbf4be0d62, byte-identical to the clip in the Command Deck store, so nothing is re-encoded and no quality is lost. At runtime the page decodes the base64 to a Blob and plays a same-origin blob: URL, falling back to a data: URI if the viewer's frame refuses the blob, and saying so in its own status line if both fail. NOT PROVEN: that a browser plays it. No browser was available; only the presence and integrity of the bytes were verified.
evidence: Build script output 2026-09-23: 'page bytes: 158484', 'embedded sha256 ok: True'; 157,956/158,484 bytes against a 16,777,216-byte cap = 0.94 %. Artifact publish versions 2 and 3, both 'readable by only you'. `node --check` of the extracted page script: JS SYNTAX OK.
fix: The page exists at https://claude.ai/artifact/EJnetbUCFscnDsDWFdp9Ti (private, newly created this session — no existing artifact was edited). Described in integrations/vanessa-voice-everywhere.md and specified for the Mac in mac-task-specs.md §6c.

area: The per-reply write path — the artifact database holds a whole clip
finding: PROVEN by execution, and it is the shape to build. A clip document of 144,825 bytes, whose `audio` field is the full 144,380-character base64 of the real clip, was written to the relay artifact's database as clip/teststeve01 and read back byte-identical: 108,284 bytes, sha256 747f8f5b...4be0d62. It read back identical a SECOND time at `as_level: "interact"`, i.e. at the access level of an ordinary signed-in viewer rather than the owner, which is the level the published page's own reader runs at. The store reported '2 of 5000 documents used in this artifact's database'. This matters because it means voice-reply-render does NOT have to learn to republish a web page: writing a clip document is the same kind of operation it already performs every ten minutes on the Command Deck store, only against a different artifact. A two-document scheme was written and verified: clip/<queue id> holds the clip, clip/newest holds {v:{id, ts}} pointing at the latest. The page resolves a `#<queue id>` fragment first so an old text keeps playing its own clip, and falls back to clip/newest. NOT PROVEN: that the fragment reaches the page. The Artifact page contract states a plain #anchor of letters, digits and . _ ~ - does reach location.hash, and queue ids are exactly that shape, but no browser was available to watch it happen — which is why the page falls back to clip/newest and, below that, to the clip built into it, so it plays something at every level of failure.
evidence: `ArtifactData` set of clip/current from a 144,825-byte local JSON file, then get with out_dir -> 144,866 bytes, version 1; local decode -> 108,284 bytes, sha256 match True. `ArtifactData` list of the clip collection at as_level 'interact' -> same document, decode -> sha256 match True. `ArtifactData` batch, 2 writes, committed atomically: set clip/teststeve01, delete clip/current. All against artifact EJnetbUCFscnDsDWFdp9Ti on 2026-09-23.

area: Retention and cost of storing a clip per reply
finding: There is a cost, it is small, and it is capped by design rather than by a cleanup job. Numbers, all measured: one clip document is about 145 KB (144,825 bytes for a 27-second reply); the relay artifact's database reported a ceiling of 5,000 documents; the page carrying a built-in clip is 158,484 bytes against a 16 MiB cap. PROPOSED CAP: keep the newest 10 clip documents plus the one-line clip/newest pointer — about 1.45 MB at rest, and at the spec's own 700-character ceiling (~67 s, ~270 KB per clip) still only ~2.7 MB. PROPOSED PRUNE: the renderer lists the clip collection after each write and deletes every clip document but the newest 10, in the same run, so there is no separate cleanup task to forget. Ten is chosen to match the cap the queue already uses — voiceReplyQueue keeps the newest 10 — so a clip exists for exactly as long as the queue item that made it. A clip older than the tenth has a dead link; that is correct behaviour for a voice note and should be stated to Steven rather than hidden, and the page says so when a fragment names a clip that is gone. The decisive cost saving is architectural: ONE artifact, republished never and written often, instead of a new artifact per reply. A new artifact per reply would leave an unbounded gallery of private pages with no prune that an agent is permitted to run, because deleting an artifact is Steven's call and not an agent's.
evidence: Measured document size 144,825 bytes written / 144,866 bytes read back; `ArtifactData` set responses reporting '1 of 5000' then '2 of 5000 documents used in this artifact's database'; page size 158,484 bytes; the 700-character / ~67 s / ~270 KB figures are from F-P5-03, not re-derived.
fix: Written into mac-task-specs.md §6c as an explicit numbered step, and into the retention paragraph of integrations/vanessa-voice-everywhere.md.

area: inkbox_media_stage — the full schema, and what it says about two P5 open items
finding: The tool's full schema was read today and it settles one P5 open question and closes off one tempting shortcut. (1) SETTLED IN PRINCIPLE: `data` accepts up to 27,962,034 characters, and the constraint that actually binds is 'the whole MCP request must stay under 1 MiB'. The full clip's base64 is 144,380 characters, about 141 KiB — inside both by a wide margin. So P5's inability to stage the complete 108,284-byte clip was a limit of THAT SESSION'S OWN OUTPUT PATH, not of the tool, and voice-reply-render on the Mac does not have that limit because it holds the bytes locally and never retypes them. It is still not EXECUTED, and is not claimed as executed. (2) CLOSED OFF: the schema also offers `source_type: "url"`, which would let Inkbox fetch a clip instead of being handed it inline — an obvious shortcut, and it does not work here, because that mode requires a URL 'publicly reachable without credentials' and artifact URLs are not (F-R4-03, proven by the failed fetch). An artifact-hosted clip can never be fed to iMessage this way. Inline base64 remains the only staging route, exactly as mac-task-specs.md §6b already says.
evidence: The `mcp__Inkbox__inkbox_media_stage` input schema as loaded on 2026-09-23: data maxLength 27962034, description 'CR/LF line wrapping is accepted; spaces, data URI prefixes, and URL-safe base64 are not, and = padding must be present ... the whole MCP request must stay under 1 MiB; use source_type url for larger files'; url description 'Must be publicly reachable without credentials'. The one url-mode call made returned url_fetch_failed.
fix: Added to the 'What is still unverified' list in integrations/vanessa-voice-everywhere.md, replacing the vaguer note about the cloud session's output path with the measured reason.

area: EMAIL — a second native-audio channel, never previously checked
finding: PROVEN, and it is the most useful thing found today. Email was treated throughout P5 as background ('Email is active') and was never tested as a delivery channel for voice — but it is live, and unlike Discord and WhatsApp it HAS an attachment parameter. `inkbox_email_attachment_upload` was called with real bytes from the clip, content_type audio/mpeg, filename vanessa-reply.mp3, and it ACCEPTED them, returning {"media_handle":"fc00c3c3-94e6-49a1-b7d0-c15d6d499e50","filename":"vanessa-reply.mp3","content_hash":"b858ecbe0a03cfd7138e4e6c11cd46cc47b75dc33c94d6ce69c98bf0528cb3bb","content_type":"audio/mpeg","size_bytes":1532,"expires_at":"2026-09-23T03:53:29.784355+00:00"}. size_bytes equals the bytes sent. The send shape is fully specified by the schemas: `inkbox_email_reply` takes message_id, approved_recipients and attachments[{media_handle, filename, content_hash, content_type}] — every one of those four fields is returned by the upload call. So Vanessa can answer an email in text AND attach her own voice, on the one identity that is already active and verified. LIMITS, measured from the schema rather than guessed: inline base64 is capped by 'the whole MCP request must stay under 1 MiB', which the full clip's ~141 KiB is well inside; a url source would allow 25 MiB but requires a PUBLIC HTTPS URL, so an artifact-hosted clip cannot be fed in that way either (F-R4-03). NOT EXECUTED: no email was sent. `inkbox_email_send` and `inkbox_email_reply` were never called — only the staging call, which by its own description copies and validates into staging 'for a later send'. The payload staged was a frame-aligned 1,532-byte prefix of the clip, not the whole 108,284 bytes, for the same reason P5 gave: a cloud session cannot faithfully retype the full base64. The ENCODING and the CONTENT TYPE are proven accepted; a full-clip stage is not claimed.
evidence: One `inkbox_email_attachment_upload` call on 2026-09-23, response quoted verbatim above. Local slice: 1,532 bytes, frame-aligned, sha256 b858ecbe0a03cfd7138e4e6c11cd46cc47b75dc33c94d6ce69c98bf0528cb3bb. `inkbox_channel_status_get` 2026-09-23: email {assigned:true, address 'jasmine@inkboxmail.com', status 'active'}, sending_domain {kind 'platform', domain 'inkboxmail.com', status 'verified'}. Schemas for inkbox_email_attachment_upload, inkbox_email_send and inkbox_email_reply read in full the same day.

area: Email staging returns a VERIFIABLE content_hash, unlike iMessage staging
finding: A difference between the two staging calls worth writing down, because P5 explicitly could not verify the iMessage one. P5 found inkbox_media_stage's content_hash matched none of sha256, sha3-256, sha512-256, blake2b-256 or blake2s of the bytes, nor sha256 of the base64, and concluded it is an opaque server token with size_bytes as the only check. The EMAIL staging call is different: inkbox_email_attachment_upload returned content_hash b858ecbe0a03cfd7138e4e6c11cd46cc47b75dc33c94d6ce69c98bf0528cb3bb, which is EXACTLY the sha256 of the 1,532 bytes sent, computed locally before the call. So on the email path the renderer can verify the staged file is its own clip by hashing its bytes and comparing, which is a stronger check than size_bytes alone. The iMessage path keeps size_bytes as its only check, exactly as §6b says.
evidence: Local hashlib.sha256 of slice.mp3 = b858ecbe0a03cfd7138e4e6c11cd46cc47b75dc33c94d6ce69c98bf0528cb3bb, printed before the call; the staging response returned the identical string as content_hash. Contrast: F-P5-01's media_stage response content_hash 10a90267d0ec932d16beaee03d89c571ea5775addeed304b87530831dcb1889d for a 12,284-byte payload, which F-P5-01 records as matching no common digest.
fix: Written into mac-task-specs.md §6d as an explicit verification step for the email path only, with a note that §6b's iMessage path cannot do the same.
